title: Neurone Structure
content:
# Neurone Structure

## Learning Objectives
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Describe the structure of sensory, relay, and motor neurones
- Explain how neurone structure is related to function
- Describe the structure and function of the myelin sheath
- Explain the role of synapses in transmitting impulses

## Introduction

**Neurones** are specialised cells that transmit electrical impulses. Their structure is highly adapted for rapid communication across long distances in the body. Understanding neurone structure helps explain how the nervous system functions.

## Key Concepts

### General Neurone Structure

**All neurones have:**

| Component | Function |
|-----------|----------|
| Cell body (soma) | Contains nucleus and organelles |
| Dendrites | Receive impulses from other neurones |
| Axon | Carries impulse away from cell body |
| Axon terminals | Pass impulse to next cell |

### The Cell Body

**Features of the cell body:**
- Contains the nucleus
- Contains many mitochondria (for energy)
- Has rough endoplasmic reticulum (for protein synthesis)
- Many ribosomes
- Also called the soma

### Dendrites

**Functions:**
- Receive impulses from other neurones
- Many branches to receive from multiple sources
- Short projections from cell body
- Increase surface area for receiving signals

### The Axon

**Features:**
- Long fibre extending from cell body
- Can be very long (up to 1 metre in some motor neurones)
- Carries impulse away from cell body
- Cytoplasm inside called axoplasm
- Membrane called axolemma

### Myelin Sheath

**What is it?**
- Fatty insulating layer around axon
- Made of Schwann cells wrapped around axon
- White in colour (gives "white matter" its name)

**Functions:**
- Electrical insulation
- Speeds up impulse transmission
- Protects the axon

[DIAGRAM: Cross-section of myelinated axon showing Schwann cells]

### Nodes of Ranvier

**What are they?**
- Gaps in the myelin sheath
- Occur at regular intervals along axon
- Expose the axon membrane

**Function:**
- Allow saltatory conduction
- Impulse "jumps" from node to node
- Much faster than continuous conduction

### Saltatory Conduction

**In myelinated neurones:**
- Impulse jumps between nodes of Ranvier
- Much faster than unmyelinated neurones
- Speed: up to 120 m/s

**In unmyelinated neurones:**
- Impulse travels continuously along axon
- Slower: about 1-2 m/s

[DIAGRAM: Saltatory conduction showing impulse jumping between nodes]

### Types of Neurone Structure

#### Sensory Neurones

**Structure:**
- Cell body located on a side branch
- Long dendron (fibre leading to cell body)
- Short axon
- One long fibre from receptor to CNS

**Function:**
- Carries impulses from receptors to CNS

[DIAGRAM: Labelled sensory neurone]

#### Relay Neurones (Interneurones)

**Structure:**
- Short neurones
- Many dendrites
- Short axon
- Cell body in middle
- Found entirely within CNS

**Function:**
- Connects sensory and motor neurones
- Processes information in CNS

[DIAGRAM: Labelled relay neurone]

#### Motor Neurones

**Structure:**
- Cell body at one end (in CNS)
- Many dendrites on cell body
- Long axon extending to effector
- Axon terminals connect to muscle fibres

**Function:**
- Carries impulses from CNS to effectors

[DIAGRAM: Labelled motor neurone]

### Comparing Neurone Types

| Feature | Sensory | Relay | Motor |
|---------|---------|-------|-------|
| Cell body position | Side branch | Central | One end |
| Dendron | Long | Short | Short |
| Axon | Short | Short | Long |
| Length | Long overall | Short | Long overall |
| Location | PNS to CNS | CNS only | CNS to PNS |
| Function | Receptor → CNS | Processing | CNS → Effector |

### Synapses

**A synapse** is the junction between two neurones.

**Structure:**
- Pre-synaptic neurone (before the gap)
- Synaptic cleft (tiny gap, ~20 nm)
- Post-synaptic neurone (after the gap)
- Synaptic vesicles (contain neurotransmitters)
- Receptor proteins on post-synaptic membrane

[DIAGRAM: Detailed structure of a synapse]

### Synaptic Transmission

**Steps:**

1. **Impulse arrives** at axon terminal of pre-synaptic neurone
2. **Calcium ions enter** the axon terminal
3. **Vesicles move** to pre-synaptic membrane
4. **Vesicles fuse** with membrane (exocytosis)
5. **Neurotransmitter released** into synaptic cleft
6. **Neurotransmitter diffuses** across cleft
7. **Binds to receptors** on post-synaptic membrane
8. **Ion channels open** in post-synaptic membrane
9. **New impulse triggered** in post-synaptic neurone
10. **Neurotransmitter removed** (broken down or reabsorbed)

### Neurotransmitters

**Common neurotransmitters:**

| Neurotransmitter | Location | Effect |
|-----------------|----------|--------|
| Acetylcholine | Neuromuscular junction | Muscle contraction |
| Noradrenaline | Sympathetic synapses | Fight or flight |
| Dopamine | Brain | Reward, movement |
| Serotonin | Brain | Mood, sleep |
| GABA | Brain | Inhibitory |

### Why Do We Need Synapses?

**Functions of synapses:**

1. **Ensure one-way transmission** - Neurotransmitter only in pre-synaptic terminal
2. **Allow integration** - Multiple inputs can be combined
3. **Allow processing** - Can amplify or inhibit signals
4. **Enable flexibility** - Pathways can be modified (learning)
5. **Filter weak signals** - Threshold must be reached

### Adaptations of Neurones

| Adaptation | Function |
|------------|----------|
| Long axons | Carry impulses over long distances |
| Myelin sheath | Fast impulse transmission |
| Many dendrites | Receive many inputs |
| Branched axon terminals | Connect to multiple cells |
| Many mitochondria | Provide ATP for active processes |
| Schwann cells | Produce myelin sheath |

## Common Exam Questions

- Label a diagram of a motor neurone
- Describe synaptic transmission
- Explain the function of the myelin sheath
- Compare sensory and motor neurones

## Common Misconceptions

- **Misconception:** Impulses travel through the synapse
- **Reality:** Electrical impulses stop at the synapse; chemical transmission takes over

- **Misconception:** All neurones look the same
- **Reality:** Different types have different structures suited to their functions

- **Misconception:** Myelin is part of the neurone
- **Reality:** Myelin is formed by separate Schwann cells wrapped around the axon

- **Misconception:** Synapses slow down transmission
- **Reality:** Yes, there's a small delay, but synapses have important functions

## Practice Questions

1. Name the part of a neurone that carries impulses away from the cell body. (1 mark)

2. State two functions of the myelin sheath. (2 marks)

3. Describe the structure of a motor neurone. (4 marks)

4. Explain how impulses cross a synapse. (4 marks)

5. Compare the structure of sensory and motor neurones. (4 marks)

6. Explain how the structure of a motor neurone is adapted to its function. (6 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Axon | Long fibre carrying impulse away from cell body |
| Dendrite | Short projection receiving impulses |
| Myelin sheath | Fatty insulating layer around axon |
| Schwann cell | Cell that produces myelin sheath |
| Node of Ranvier | Gap in myelin sheath |
| Synapse | Junction between two neurones |
| Neurotransmitter | Chemical that transmits signal across synapse |
| Synaptic cleft | Gap between neurones at synapse |
| Saltatory conduction | Impulse jumping between nodes of Ranvier |

## Summary

- Neurones have cell body, dendrites, axon, and axon terminals
- Sensory neurones: cell body on side branch, carry impulses to CNS
- Motor neurones: long axon, cell body at one end, carry impulses to effectors
- Relay neurones: short, found in CNS, connect sensory to motor
- Myelin sheath insulates axon and speeds up transmission
- Synapses are junctions where chemical transmission occurs
- Neurotransmitters cross the synaptic cleft and trigger new impulses
